UserPromptSubmit.description: Surface newly-tapped status-board answers into context. The board records answers server-side and notifies nobody; relying on the agent to remember to read the file failed within an hour of the rule being written. Durable but slow: it can only fire when the owner sends a message, so a tap waits for their next prompt. The waiter (hooks/answer-waiter.py, registered on this event too, on SessionStart and on Stop) is the fast path and removes that latency — keep both, they fail differently. Both take their answers from status-board/answer_ledger.py, which marks what it hands out under one lock, so an answer is told once, whichever path got to it first. This hook also says to the agent, once, when no waiter is running for the session. Silent in a worker that Orca dispatched (hooks/orca_session.py): the answers are for the session that keeps the board, and a worker that read them also marked them surfaced, hiding them from the coordinator.

Fast path for status-board answers: waits in the background and wakes the session within seconds of a tap (asyncRewake: exit 2 wakes Claude immediately even when the session is idle; measured 14 Nov 2026, 0.06 s to a new turn). Started on SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and Stop, so it runs again after every turn with nothing asked of the agent; Stop alone misses a turn the owner interrupts. `async` is set as well as `asyncRewake` so that a Claude Code which ignored asyncRewake would still background it rather than block the end of a turn. `timeout` is 21 days (1 814 400 s), above the waiter's own deadline of 21 days minus an hour, so Claude Code never kills it, and under the 2^31-1 ms that a JavaScript timer can hold (Claude Code 2.1.325 clamps a longer one and logs it; a hook with timeout 20 was killed at 20 s, so the figure is enforced: spike of 14 Nov 2026). A session can sit idle for days and its keeper must still be woken by the owner's tap. After 21 days with no hook the waiter ends; the owner is then told by the other sessions that an answer waits unheard (hooks/board-answers.py). Replaces the Monitor watcher, which could not be armed as instructed (no `persistent` option), ended after 30 minutes, and made /restart refuse; a waiting hook does not. Shares the seen-marker with board-answers.py under one lock. Claims nothing when its session was restarted (/restart re-execs Claude Code in place and leaves a deaf waiter behind): see the file. Silent in a worker that Orca dispatched.

SessionStart.description: The answer waiter, started with the session (startup, resume, clear, compact), so an answer that lands while nothing is waiting is delivered at once and a restarted session gets a waiter that can reach it: a waiter from before /restart survives it but is deaf. See the entry on UserPromptSubmit. Replaces the instruction to arm a Monitor watcher, which the agent could not follow as described and which was not given at all on a board with no answers yet.

Offer the bootstrap in a folder with no team structure. A new session in a new folder never suggested /project-bootstrap, so the working practice this plugin exists to provide arrived only if the owner remembered to ask. A hook cannot run a skill, only instruct the agent, so this is an instruction — and it insists on the order: ask what the project is and who works on it, get a yes, only then scaffold. Silent when .claude/rules/team-roles.md exists at the cwd or its git top-level (a bare .claude/ proves nothing: Claude Code creates settings.local.json itself), in $HOME, / and ~/.claude, on resume/compact/fork, in an agent session, and when opted out (PROJECT_INIT_NO_OFFER=1, or an empty .claude/no-bootstrap-offer). Fails quiet: any error prints nothing and exits 0, so a bug costs the offer, not the session. A pane teammate is recognised by agent_type/agent_id, or by --agent-id/--parent-session-id on an ancestor process; neither has been seen in a live teammate yet, so one may still see the offer — noise, not damage. An Orca worker is a plain claude process with neither tell; it is recognised from a dispatch that Orca lists as still live on its terminal (hooks/orca_session.py), on one observation that the record exists before SessionStart. A settled worker's terminal does not count.

Restart a project's status board that is not running. A board's state survives a reboot but its server does not, and the owner found out by opening a dead URL. If the project has a board and nothing answers on its port (derived by serve.py itself — imported, not copied, so the two cannot disagree), this starts serve.py detached, logging to boards/<slug>/serve.log, and prints the URL. It does nothing if the board page already answers; if something else holds the port it starts nothing and says so in one line. Fails quiet but not blind: it always exits 0 and never waits more than a few seconds, and when it cannot bring the board up it prints one line pointing at the log. Limits: it restarts with serve.py's defaults (loopback only; the folder name as display name, since serve.py stores none), and it cannot tell another project's board on the same derived port from this one.

Stop.description: The answer waiter again, after every turn of the agent: the waiter ends when it wakes the session, when it is replaced, and at its deadline, and this starts the next one with nothing asked of the agent. See the entry on UserPromptSubmit.

PostToolUse.description: Record which session writes the board, so that only it is told the owner's answers (the owner's ruling, 14 Nov 2026: the session that last wrote the board's content; another session that takes the board over becomes the one that is told). Runs only for a write to a board's narrative.json: the `if` rule keeps every other Write free. A Write has its own rule: an Edit(...) rule does not match a Write (measured 14 Nov 2026, Claude Code 2.1.325).
Same, for the Edit tool (the Edit rule applies to the other editing tools too, by the documentation; only Edit itself was run).

hooks.command: p=$(cat); case "$p" in *narrative.json*) printf '%s' "$p" | python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/board-keeper.py";; esac

PostToolUse.description: The end of a Bash call that names narrative.json (cat, cp, tee, a script's argument, a `>` redirect or a heredoc): its session is recorded as the board's writer only if the file changed during this very call and no other session's call that named it could have changed it (see PreToolUse). It has no `if` rule on purpose: a `>` redirect's target is not part of what a Bash rule sees (measured 14 Nov 2026), so a rule could never see `cat > narrative.json`. The shell `case` starts no Python for a payload that does not mention the file (about 6 ms per Bash call, in every session; Python's own start-up is 30 ms); the hook checks the command text itself, since the payload also holds the output. A script that writes the file without naming it records nobody, and neither does the owner's editor: there is no sweep at the end of the turn (the review of 14 Nov 2026, findings 2 and 3).

hooks.command: p=$(cat); case "$p" in *narrative.json*) printf '%s' "$p" | python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/board-keeper.py";; esac

PreToolUse.description: The start of a Bash call that names narrative.json: stores the file's signature, so that the end of the call (PostToolUse) can tell whether this call changed it. A Bash call's Pre and Post carry the same tool_use_id, Pre first, for a session and for a subagent too (spike of 14 Nov 2026, Claude Code 2.1.325). Same shell test as there: no Python for a command that does not mention the file.

Deny a dispatch that would grant a second agent the working tree while another already holds it — "one agent owns the working tree at a time" was already written in team-roles.md and verification.md and was broken twice anyway, including once while the lead was actively quoting it. A rule that has been read and re-broken is proof the rule is the wrong instrument; this is the mechanism instead. Silent for a dispatch that is not tree-mutating (repo-inventory, architect, qa), for isolation: "worktree" dispatches, and for a role resuming itself. See status-board/tree_lock.py for the lock state both this hook and the board read.
